summaries.one_paragraph_summary: The prompt_contract phase preserved the original Waypoint prompt verbatim and converted it into a full execution contract: hard requirements (SwiftUI/SwiftData/MapKit/ActivityKit/EventKit/WidgetKit only, no backend/accounts/third-party SDKs, no faked network-dependent behavior), explicit non-goals (no cloud sync, no real-time traffic/flight data, no hidden sharing layer), a production-readiness definition centered on deterministic behavior and honest permission degradation, and 32 numbered testable requirements traceable one-to-one to the original prompt's clauses. QA/skeptic review then hardened the three highest-risk areas into concrete, resolved decision rules rather than leaving them as later-phase judgment calls: settlement must be genuine minimum-transaction debt-simplification (not just correct net balances) with a deterministic remainder-cent rule (assigned to the payer) and a code-level sum-identity check; cross-day drag-and-drop must be atomic with no orphaned/duplicated stops, preserving a moved stop's time window but visually flagging it if it falls outside the new day's normal range; and every permission/capability-gated feature (Live Activity, Calendar export, MapKit routing) must degrade honestly with degradation verified by actually observing the denied/unavailable state, not inferred from code. Additional resolved assumptions: CloudKit sync is off by default and undocumented sync is forbidden; Live Activity updates must be local/scheduled-only with no push/server mechanism; the demo trip must carry a visible 'Demo' marker distinct from real data; Calendar export dedup uses a stored EventKit identifier per stop with lookup-and-update on re-export; iPad split view must be verified as genuinely independent two-pane interaction across sizes/orientations, not just API usage. The group reached consensus with no unresolved disagreements — Claude's contributions were additive refinements to Codex's contract rather than contradictions.
open_risks: MKDirections and EventKit/Calendar behavior in the iOS Simulator may not be fully deterministic across environments, making some degradation paths hard to reproduce consistently during verification.
Live Activities cannot be fully visually verified in the Simulator the way they render on a physical Dynamic Island, limiting how conclusively that feature can be confirmed pre-device-testing.

Debt-simplification correctness with realistic multi-traveler, multi-expense scenarios (not just 2-3 person toy cases) needs deliberate adversarial test data in a later phase to actually catch a naive implementation.
iPad split-view verification requires deliberate multi-size/orientation/Slide-Over testing that could be skipped if a later phase only checks compile success.

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: Both agents converged without real disagreement on Waypoint's product research: the audience is small groups/couples/families planning multi-day trips together who want a single offline no-account tool in place of a fragmented Notes+spreadsheet+Splitwise workflow (ASSUMPTION, no live user research), with the important caveat named plainly that 'no accounts/no sync' makes this a single-device/single-owner tool despite 'expense splitting' sounding inherently collaborative. Comparable patterns cited (ASSUMPTION/pattern-level, not fetched-source-backed) are TripIt, Google Maps timeline, Splitwise, and Wanderlog as the closest all-in-one competitor; the exploitable gap against all of them is that they're cloud/account-dependent and degrade badly offline, while Waypoint's differentiator is staying genuinely offline-first while still getting debt-simplification and cross-day drag-reorder integrity fully correct rather than faked. Platform-opportunity analysis flagged Live Activity as the highest native-feel payoff but also the hardest to verify (Dynamic Island rendering can't be confirmed outside physical hardware, so verification claims must stay explicitly bounded), the widget's refresh-budget staleness needing honest framing in copy, and iPad split view being a premium differentiator only if genuinely independent-pane. Concrete risks converted into build implications: settlement math needs adversarial testing (4+ travelers, excluded payer, non-100%-summing percentages) since naive implementations pass 2-3 person happy paths and fail only at scale; drag-reorder across days needs repeated-drag testing including empty-day and last-stop-removal cases, not a single clean demo; and MapKit's 'offline-cached' framing is optimistic for first-visit locations, so the straight-line approximate-route fallback should be treated as the expected default path in review, with the seeded demo trip required to include at least one stop that can't resolve a route so this differentiator is actually visible. Both agents independently arrived at the same first-build sequencing: trips/days/stops/reorder and settlement math first, then calendar export dedup and iPad split view, then Live Activity and widget last as status surfaces layered onto an already-proven-consistent trip-state model.
open_risks: The single-device/no-sync nature of expense splitting is a real UX friction point for actual multi-person groups that no amount of clever settlement math resolves — it needs to be framed honestly in onboarding rather than discovered as a disappointment.

Competitor and pattern claims (TripIt, Google Maps, Splitwise, Wanderlog feature sets) are ASSUMPTION-labeled without a live fetched source, so specifics could be stale or inaccurate if precision on competitor features becomes important later.

Live Activity and widget verification will remain bounded by simulator/no-hardware limits through the whole project; later phases must keep stating this honestly rather than letting confidence creep upward as code volume increases.

MapKit's first-visit-location network dependency was reasoned about, not empirically tested against real Simulator network conditions yet — this should be confirmed rather than assumed once build-verification begins.

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: Both agents independently and without disagreement concluded that Waypoint is a single-app build, not a portfolio: the prompt names one cohesive product, and the contract's hardest guarantees (genuine minimum-transaction debt-simplification settlement, atomic no-orphan/no-duplicate cross-day drag-reorder, and identifier-based calendar-export dedup) all depend on a single shared SwiftData model for trips/days/stops/travelers/expenses, which would be undermined by splitting into sibling apps per feature area. The selected app is Waypoint (category: Travel Planning, slug `waypoint`, build=true), targeting small groups/couples/families who want one local-first tool for itinerary, mapping, expense settlement, packing, and calendar export instead of a fragmented Notes+spreadsheet+Splitwise workflow, with the single-device/no-sync nature of shared data to be stated honestly in the product rather than implied away. No portfolio-json manifest was produced since no split applies. Claude additionally emphasized, as a carried-forward product framing rather than a contested point, that the itinerary/day/stop model and settlement math are structurally load-bearing and should never be the thing simplified under time pressure — if scope must be trimmed later, it should be a surface feature (Live Activity, widget) documented as bounded/unverifiable-in-simulator, not the core trip-state model.

Both agents converged tightly on a unified product promise for Waypoint: a single-device, fully offline iOS app giving a trip owner (the one person in a couple/family/friend group who organizes and carries the phone) one trustworthy local data model spanning itinerary, map routing, expense settlement, and packing, with zero accounts/backend/sync. The key IA decision, contributed primarily by Claude and unopposed, is that the day view (synced stop list + map) is the app's center of gravity rather than the trips list, because the highest-stakes moment is mid-trip with weak signal, not pre-trip planning — packing and calendar export are lower-frequency actions nested one level down, not co-equal tabs, and a trip-switcher stays reachable from the day view so multi-trip users aren't trapped. Hard scope boundaries were locked explicitly: no accounts/backend/third-party SDKs/login, no sync of any kind (including anything resembling AirDrop/share-sheet live sync), no real-time data (traffic/flights/weather) even as a stretch goal, and no cross-device collaborative editing — any future sharing-adjacent feature requires its own explicit decision. The demo trip must remain strictly a Settings toggle, never silently seeded as onboarding content; a brand-new user's first launch must show genuinely honest empty states. Success criteria were defined adversarially rather than as a feature checklist: correct day math across all date-range shapes, a stop surviving 20 repeated cross-day drags with no duplication/loss as a single atomic operation, settle-up with 5+ travelers and uneven splits producing the exact minimum-transaction count with cent-exact sums, idempotent EventKit export, genuinely independent iPad two-pane interaction, and every permission-gated feature (Live Activity, Calendar, MapKit routing) actually observed failing gracefully rather than merely coded defensively. No disagreement surfaced in this phase — it was an alignment round confirming and sharpening decisions already implicit in prompt_contract and product_research.

The product brief for Waypoint is locked: the paying user is a repeat multi-day-group-trip planner (not a one-off single-trip user), and the app's paid value is a single trip-count gate rather than a feature menu — free tier is exactly one active trip with everything on it fully correct (all stops, all travelers, real Decimal-based minimum-transaction settlement math, honest MapKit degradation with visible approximate-route labeling, packing checklist, and the full iPad split view), while Pro (offered as both an annual subscription and a lifetime non-consumable purchase in the same StoreKit product group, explicitly rejecting subscription-only billing for a serverless static-content app) adds unlimited concurrent trips, saved/reusable packing templates, EventKit calendar export, Live Activity, the home-screen widget, and settlement audit-log/category-spend-breakdown reporting. Traveler count is never capped and settlement correctness, the iPad split view, and honest map-degradation fallback behavior are never paywalled at any tier, since gating those would directly contradict the app's core trust pitch. A lapsed subscription or failed restore never deletes, hides, or corrupts existing trip data — it only locks new-trip creation past the free cap and Pro-only surfaces. The core loop centers the day view (stop list + map, check off, reorder, log expenses, settle up) as a trip command center, with packing and calendar export as lower-frequency pre/post-trip actions. The competitive wedge is provably correct offline behavior under adversity versus cloud-account-dependent competitors (TripIt, Wanderlog, Splitwise). The growth mechanic is a one-way, explicitly labeled 'Trip Snapshot' export (PDF/text/.ics) defaulting to itinerary-only content, with expense/settlement data excluded unless the owner explicitly opts in, to avoid an unintended financial-privacy leak to non-paying recipients. Local-first behavior remains the default (SwiftData-only, CloudKit off by default, no accounts, explicit visible status on any denied/unavailable permission or capability), with cloud sync reserved as a documented, explicit v2 opt-in built on a sync-ready-but-inactive schema (optional relationships, no unique constraints, default values) rather than a default or assumed future.
open_risks: StoreKit product configuration for a dual annual-subscription-plus-lifetime-purchase model in the same subscription group needs concrete App Store Connect setup validation in the build phase, since this is a slightly less common configuration than pure subscription or pure one-time purchase.

The settlement audit-log/category-spend-breakdown Pro feature still needs a concrete design (what categories, how they're assigned to expenses) before it can be built — it was agreed to conceptually but not specified in detail.

Free-tier 'one active trip' needs a precise definition of what happens to a second trip a free user creates (blocked at creation, or created but read-only, or trip-switau interrupts) — this phase decided the gate exists but not its exact UX mechanics, which the design/build phases must specify.

Downgrade/lapse behavior is specified at the policy level (no data loss, lock new creation and Pro surfaces) but the exact UI treatment of a locked feature (e.g., grayed-out vs. hidden vs. upsell-on-tap) is left to a later design phase.

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: With Codex's CLI unavailable this round, Claude produced a solo but thorough proposal for Waypoint's smallest valuable slice, adopted as the phase decision since it satisfied both acceptance checks and contradicted nothing locked in prior phases. The MVP slice is a single end-to-end workflow: create a trip with correct date-range math (including single-day trips), land on a day view with ordered timed/annotated stops synced two-way to a MapKit view, drag-reorder stops within a day and across days, see honest MKDirections routing or a visibly-labeled approximate straight-line fallback, log expenses against travelers across all three split methods (equal/exact/percentage), and see a settle-up screen compute genuine minimum-transaction debt-simplification with cent-exact rounding. The demo trip Settings toggle ships as part of this slice (not deferred), carrying its required visible 'Demo' marker and at least one deliberately unresolvable-route stop so the approximate fallback is actually observed. Explicitly cut from this slice, named as future work rather than stretch goals: Live Activity, the home-screen widget, EventKit calendar export, packing lists/templates, the iPad two-pane split view, and all StoreKit/paywall code. Two implementation constraints were locked as non-negotiable even at this reduced scope: cross-day drag must be a single atomic SwiftData operation from the first build (never a naive delete-then-insert retrofitted later), and settlement must be the real greedy debt-simplification algorithm with an in-code sum-identity assertion from the first build (never a placeholder stub) — because faking either would validate the wrong thing. Validation criteria for this slice are adversarial, not happy-path: 10+ rapid cross-day drags with no duplication/loss, a 5-traveler mixed-split settle-up producing a minimal transaction count with cent-exact sums, and an observed (not just coded) approximate-route fallback on a forced MKDirections failure.
open_risks: Codex did not weigh in this round due to CLI unavailability, so this slice definition has not had a genuine second-agent adversarial pass — a future phase or build-verification step should sanity-check it isn't missing something a second perspective would have caught.

The validation criteria (10+ drags, 5-traveler settle-up, forced routing failure) are specified as manual/adversarial test scenarios but not yet codified as automated tests; build-verification must actually execute them, not just reference them.

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: With Codex again unavailable (rate-limited), Claude's solo skeptic pass resolved six previously-implicit seams left open by earlier phases, adopted as the phase's working decisions since none contradict prior locked decisions and each closes a concrete ambiguity rather than restating known requirements. Trip date-range shrinking that would orphan stops on removed days now blocks the edit and surfaces the affected stops, rather than risking a silent cascade-delete; extending a range stays unrestricted. Percentage splits that don't sum to 100% are rejected at entry with an inline error rather than silently auto-rescaled, extending the honesty principle to expense-entry validation. Drag-and-drop reordering now requires a parallel non-gesture 'Move to...' action routed through the identical atomic SwiftData operation, closing an accessibility gap (VoiceOver users cannot reliably drag) without introducing a second, divergent code path that could reintroduce duplication bugs. The demo trip is now specified as a singleton keyed by a stable identifier so repeated toggle on/off/on cycles can never create duplicate demo trips or touch real user data. Stop times are scoped to the device's current local timezone always, with true destination-timezone-aware itineraries named explicitly as a Gap, closing a previously undecided ambiguity around trips that cross timezones and its effect on Live Activity's 'is the trip active today' logic. Finally, the debug current-date injection hook from DEC-prompt_contract-009 must be compiled out of release builds via #if DEBUG rather than only hidden behind a settings flag, since a discoverable flag-only gate could let a real build be forced into a fake 'active trip' state.
open_risks: Codex has now missed two consecutive phases (next_steps_small and this one) due to rate-limiting/CLI unavailability; a growing share of the project's detailed decisions have had no genuine second-agent adversarial pass, which is worth flagging to a human reviewer rather than continuing to silently treat solo output as consensus.

The accessible 'Move to...' reorder action and the timezone/local-time scoping are new requirements that must be reflected in the build phase's task breakdown — they weren't part of the next_steps_small MVP slice definition and could be missed if that slice's requirement list isn't revisited.

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: With Codex unavailable a third consecutive round, Claude's solo pragmatist pass produced the phase's MoSCoW scoring, adopted as the working decision since it only prioritizes already-locked scope rather than introducing new requirements. Must-have: the full trip/day/stop/reorder/map/settlement core loop, the trip date-range shrink guard, the demo-trip singleton toggle, 'honest degradation' elevated to its own explicit acceptance bar (rather than implicit per-feature), the packing checklist with packed-percentage, calendar export with its already-fully-specified identifier-based dedup, and the iPad two-pane split view with its already-locked independent-pane verification bar. Should-have: Live Activity/Dynamic Island and the home-screen widget (both carry a named unverifiable-without-hardware ceiling, so a smaller fully-verified app is preferred over a half-verified version of these per the global 'smaller finished app' rule) and packing templates (introduces template-vs-instance data-model risk not required for single-trip usefulness). Could-have: StoreKit/Pro-tier paywall wiring, the Trip Snapshot export, and settlement audit-log/category-spend reporting — monetization and reporting layers on an already-correct free experience. Won't-build, explicitly named for the Gaps section: CloudKit/iCloud sync, any AirDrop/share-sheet live-sync-alike mechanism, real-time traffic/flight/weather data, cross-device collaborative editing, and destination-timezone-aware itineraries. A 46-item numbered requirements-json contract was produced mapping every testable promise (30 core, 16 non-core) for the adherence gate to grade against. The key judgment call this phase made and defended explicitly: 'named in the original prompt' does not automatically mean must-have — the must/should split is driven by whether cutting a feature breaks the app's honesty/trust pitch versus whether it merely can't be conclusively verified in this build environment, and if scope must be trimmed under time pressure, Live Activity/widget/templates are named as the correct place to trim first, never the core trip-state or settlement model.
open_risks: Codex has now missed three consecutive phases (next_steps_small, detailed_discussion, app_features) due to rate-limiting/CLI unavailability; the project's scope and prioritization decisions have had no genuine second-agent adversarial pass across this entire stretch, which is worth flagging to a human reviewer before the build phase locks in this MoSCoW list.

The interaction between must-have features (e.g. calendar export, packing templates) and the could-have StoreKit Pro-tier gating from per_app_product_brief is not fully resolved here — this phase scored build priority, not which tier each feature ships behind, so the build phase should confirm whether must-have features can ship functionally complete but gated, or ungated until StoreKit work happens.

The should-have demotion of Live Activity/widget is a judgment call, not something Codex verified independently; if a future phase or reviewer disagrees that verification-ceiling risk justifies demoting explicitly-named prompt features, this scoring may need revisiting.

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: With Codex unavailable a fourth consecutive round, Claude's solo design pass defined Waypoint's full visual and interaction language, adopted as the phase decision since it satisfies all required outputs and acceptance checks without contradicting prior locked scope. The design language is 'Trail Ledger' — warm paper-toned backgrounds, ink/forest text, a brass/amber accent replacing system blue, and tabular monospaced numerals for all times and money — chosen specifically because the app's credibility rests on itinerary integrity and settlement math being provably correct, which a ledger/logbook visual grammar expresses directly. The emotional target for the day view (already the app's IA hub) is feeling like a captain glancing at a logbook that's always right. The signature interaction is the cross-day drag rendered as a ledger page opening to receive a moved stop and snapping shut with haptic feedback, so the animation itself visibly demonstrates the atomic-move guarantee at every frame. The default SwiftUI-list/system-blue/stock-pin/plain-form look is explicitly rejected in favor of four named replacements: ticket-stub stop cards, a brass/amber accent throughout, custom category-keyed map pin shapes, and a live-updating running balance preview during expense entry. A full screen inventory and navigation flow was locked (trip switcher → day view hub with ribbon/list/map → stop detail sheet, trip create/edit with an inline shrink-guard, travelers/expense/settle-up via a persistent toolbar, packing checklist, calendar export confirmation, settings, Live Activity/widget), along with concrete state-model specifics: the demo trip gets a distinct tab color plus a literal 'DEMO' stamp graphic (not just text), settle-up shows audit-style arithmetic proving its sums rather than just a final answer, and calendar re-export shows explicit created/updated counts with distinct copy per failure mode rather than generic messages. Accessibility requirements were made concrete: 'Move to...' is a first-class context-menu action (not hidden in edit mode), custom map pins carry real accessibility labels, card contrast must be verified in both light and dark, and Dynamic Type must reflow cards taller rather than ever truncating a time or dollar amount. The coordinator resolved the one open question Claude flagged in its own pass — how the day ribbon behaves on long trips — by deciding it switches to a compact numeral-only scroll mode past 7 days.
open_risks: Codex has now missed four consecutive phases (next_steps_small, detailed_discussion, app_features, design_discussion) due to rate-limiting/CLI unavailability; the app's entire visual/interaction design has had no genuine second-agent adversarial pass, which is worth flagging to a human reviewer before build begins.

The paper-texture/ledger styling introduces real contrast and Dynamic Type risk that was named as launch-blocking in this phase but has not yet been empirically verified — build-verification must actually check contrast ratios and Dynamic Type reflow, not just accept the design intent.
The 7-day ribbon threshold for switching to compact numeral mode is a reasonable but untested judgment call, picked to close an open question rather than validated against real long-trip usage.

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: With Codex unavailable a fifth consecutive round, Claude's solo pass produced Waypoint's complete design handoff spec, adopted as the phase decision since it meets all five required acceptance checks (zero invented Theme.swift values, named components with real state variants per screen, full light/dark on every color role, no hidden decisions, category-specific premium direction). The full 'Trail Ledger' token set is locked: an explicit type scale (including a dedicated tabular Ledger Numeral style for all times/money), an 8pt spacing grid, a light/dark semantic color palette (warm paper/ink-brown backgrounds, brass/amber accent replacing system blue, a forest tone kept visually distinct for success/positive-balance states, warning/error roles), and three named corner-radius steps plus a custom TicketStubBackground shape for the perforated card edge. Navigation is locked as a non-tab-bar NavigationStack/NavigationSplitView rooted at the trip switcher, with the critical detail that the iPad two-pane split activates only inside the day view (not app-wide) to avoid accidentally violating the iPad independent-pane requirement from prompt_contract. Two concrete engineering risks were surfaced and resolved: the two-way map-pin/list-row selection must use a single @State source of truth (never dual-synced state) to avoid desync bugs, and the cross-day drag's page-flip animation must be sequenced strictly after the underlying SwiftData write completes so the animation can never visually claim success ahead of a real write. A ten-component inventory was locked and mapped to screens, a real per-screen state matrix was defined (settle-up gets three distinct states, calendar export gets four, map view distinguishes loading from approximate-fallback), and motion/haptics timing was pinned to specific triggers rather than left as vague guidance. A cross-target sharing requirement was named: Theme.swift and shared components must live in a package importable by the main app, widget, and Live Activity targets from the start, or the demo marker will visually drift across surfaces and break an earlier locked requirement. No external Claude Design pass was deemed necessary; an optional, non-blocking illustration pass was named for two purely graphical elements only, with a fully sufficient SF Symbols/hand-coded fallback if skipped.
open_risks: Codex has now missed five consecutive phases (next_steps_small through design_handoff) due to rate-limiting/CLI unavailability; the app's entire design language, screen architecture, and now the full implementation-ready spec have had no genuine second-agent adversarial pass across the whole design track — worth surfacing to a human reviewer before build begins in earnest.

The WCAG contrast requirement on the paper/ink-brown color pairing is specified as a build-blocking check but has not been empirically verified against the actual hex values chosen in this phase; build-verification must run real contrast calculations, not just accept the design intent.

The shared-package requirement for cross-target token/component reuse (widget + Live Activity) is a real Xcode project-structure decision that the build phase must set up correctly from its first commit — if the project is scaffolded with the widget/Live Activity as fully isolated targets without a shared sources group from day one, retrofitting it later is meaningfully more expensive than doing it right at setup.

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: With Codex unavailable a sixth consecutive round, Claude's solo architecture pass produced Waypoint's implementation-level technical architecture, adopted as the phase decision since it satisfies all required outputs (SwiftUI architecture, framework choices, persistence plan, permissions plan, dependency decision, testing implications) without contradicting prior locked scope — and it corrects one real latent error: Live Activity is not a fourth Xcode target but is declared inside the same WidgetKit extension target as the home-screen widget via ActivityConfiguration, meaning the project has two targets total (app + widget extension), not three. The data model is pinned concretely: Day is a real SwiftData @Model (never a computed grouping) so empty days and drag targets have somewhere to anchor, each Stop carries an explicit sortIndex:Int rather than trusting relationship array order, and both the drag gesture and the accessible 'Move to...' menu call one identical atomic moveStop(_:to:at:) function with rollback-on-failure. Views use @Query directly with no per-screen ViewModel layer; mutation logic centralizes in plain ModelContext-parameterized services (StopReorderService, SettlementEngine, CalendarExportService, DemoSeeder), which double as the unit-test seam. Settlement arithmetic moves to integer minor units (cents) internally, converting to Decimal only at the persistence/display boundary, turning the sum-identity assertion into a trivial integer equality. Permissions were tightened: no location permission is requested at all in v1 (MKDirections doesn't need the user's position), Calendar uses full-access (not write-only) since the dedup mechanism requires identifier lookup, and ActivityKit requests are gated on areActivitiesEnabled with pushType:nil named as a literal build-verification grep target. Two cross-process correctness risks were closed: the #if DEBUG current-date hook must live in an App Group UserDefaults suite (not an in-process variable) so the main app and widget extension processes agree on 'today' during verification, and the same App Group serves the widget's SwiftData access via ModelConfiguration(groupContainer:). The demo trip's unresolvable-route stop must use structurally unroutable coordinates (open ocean) rather than depending on a genuine live network failure, so the approximate-fallback differentiator is deterministic on every review regardless of Simulator network conditions. The free-tier 'one active trip' gate finally got an operational definition (current trip count, enforced at creation, no isLocked flag) with a bundled .storekit configuration file required from day one. Testing strategy explicitly avoids flaky XCUITest drag simulation for the repeated-move regression test in favor of driving it through the identical-function 'Move to...' path, reserving manual verification for the actual drag gesture; a PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy manifest was flagged as a required, easy-to-add-now artifact.
open_risks: Codex has now missed six consecutive phases due to rate-limiting/CLI unavailability; the entire design and architecture track has had no genuine second-agent adversarial pass, which is worth surfacing to a human reviewer before tech_specs locks implementation details in stone.

The App Group entitlement and shared ModelConfiguration(groupContainer:) setup is a real Xcode project-configuration step that must be done correctly at initial scaffolding — if the project is set up without it and the widget/debug-hook work is retrofitted later, reconciling two already-diverging SwiftData stores is significantly more expensive.

The integer-minor-units settlement engine design is sound but has not yet been exercised against the specific adversarial test cases (4+ travelers, excluded payer, non-100%-summing percentages) named in product_research and next_steps_small — build-verification must confirm the integer approach actually produces the correct minimum-transaction result under those cases, not just that it sums exactly.

Manually-verified-only coverage of the actual finger-drag gesture (as opposed to the Move-to path) means a real regression in drag-specific code (vs. Move-to-specific code) could slip past automated CI between review cycles.

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: With Codex unavailable a seventh consecutive round, Claude's solo pass turned ios_architecture_review's high-level architecture into a fully buildable module boundary and complete type contract for Waypoint, adopted as the phase decision since it satisfies all required outputs (architecture overview, file/module layout, data models, persistence strategy, testing strategy, interfaces-json) and its own Red Team requirement. The project structure is locked as one Xcode project with two targets (Waypoint app, WaypointWidget extension) plus a local Swift Package WaypointKit imported by both, holding the SwiftData schema, Theme.swift, shared components, and plain services, with a shared-sources file group named as the fallback if local-package-with-@Model friction appears. The full SwiftData schema was pinned (Trip/Day/Stop/Traveler/Expense/ExpenseSplit/PackingItem/PackingTemplate/PackingTemplateItem), with money stored as Int cents at rest (not just computed transiently) so the sum-identity check is a standing data-integrity property, and Stop.day kept non-optional as the literal enforcement point of the atomic-move invariant. The phase's required Red Team catch was applied and resolved in the same pass: deleting a Traveler already tied to an expense was completely unguarded, mirroring the day-shrink-orphan risk on a different axis, and is now blocked via a new TravelerDeletionGuard that surfaces the specific blocking expenses. A versioned Schema/SchemaMigrationPlan (WaypointSchemaV1) was locked from day one to avoid a destructive-reinstall crisis across the multiple remaining build slices. Concurrency boundaries were made explicit: StopReorderService/SettlementEngine stay synchronous/main-actor on model objects, while CalendarExportService/MKDirections extract Sendable DTOs before crossing await boundaries and apply results back on the main actor, since SwiftData model objects are unsafe to hold across awaited system calls. A deliberate simplicity call was made to avoid relationship-traversing #Predicate @Query given the app's inherently small data scale, and a widgetURL deep link was locked as the baseline correctness bar for the already-committed widget feature. Testing strategy gained two new adversarial cases: an automated traveler-deletion-guard test and an 8-traveler/40-expense stress-scale settlement correctness check.
open_risks: Codex has now missed seven consecutive phases due to rate-limiting/CLI unavailability; the entire design, architecture, and now full tech-spec track has had no genuine second-agent adversarial pass across the whole project — this should be surfaced to a human reviewer before build begins in earnest, since tech_specs is the last phase before implementation starts.

The local-SPM-package-with-@Model-types-shared-across-two-targets approach is flagged by Claude itself as not bulletproof in Xcode; if it hits real friction during project scaffolding, the team must actually fall back to the shared-sources-group alternative rather than losing time fighting the package configuration.

The newly-introduced TravelerDeletionGuard and the versioned SchemaMigrationPlan are both first-time requirements at this phase with no prior-phase precedent to check against — the build phase should treat them as first-class must-implement items rather than easy-to-drop nice-to-haves given they closed real integrity/maintainability gaps.

The stress-trip perf/settlement test (30 days x 10 stops, 8 travelers, 40 expenses) is specified as a requirement but its actual pass/fail threshold for 'stays snappy' was not quantified — build-verification should either quantify this or treat it as a correctness-only check without an implied performance SLA.

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: With Codex unavailable an eighth consecutive round, Claude's solo systems/backend-skeptic pass produced Waypoint's build sequencing as ten dependency-ordered milestones (M0-M9), adopted as the phase decision since it satisfies the phase's required outputs (milestones, dependencies, risk mitigations, verification plan) and closes one genuine cross-phase gap rather than merely restating prior decisions. M0 is pure scaffolding: both Xcode targets stood up for real (not stubbed), the App Group entitlement wired, and the WaypointKit local-package-with-@Model-across-two-targets approach actually attempted early with an immediate shared-sources-group fallback if it fails — this exact risk had been flagged as unvalidated across two prior phases without ever being tried. M1 delivers the core trip/day/stop model and atomic reorder together with its adversarial 10x/20x cross-day regression test in the same milestone, not after. M2 (day view UI) also builds TripGateChecker hardcoded to isPro=false so gating logic isn't built twice later, and resolves a previously-undecided gap: the free-tier one-trip cap counts non-demo trips only, making the demo toggle fully orthogonal to monetization in both directions. M3 through M8 sequence money/settlement (with its adversarial test set required for sign-off), packing, calendar export, iPad split view, Live Activity/widget, and StoreKit in that order, each carrying forward its already-locked adversarial verification bar. M9 is explicitly scoped as build-verification that actually triggers every permission/capability degradation path rather than reviewing guard-clause code, and — because Codex has now missed every phase from next_steps_small onward — is named as the project's first real adversarial pass on the entire accumulated decision set, not routine final polish.
open_risks: Codex has now missed eight consecutive phases due to rate-limiting/CLI unavailability; the entire product, design, architecture, tech-spec, and now project-plan track has had no genuine second-agent adversarial pass, placing unusually high weight on M9 (build-verification) to catch anything a second perspective would have caught earlier.

The WaypointKit local-SPM-package validation is scheduled for M0 but its outcome (package vs. shared-sources fallback) is not yet known — later milestones' file/module organization assumptions depend on which path is actually taken.

The demo-trip-vs-monetization-gate resolution (non-demo trips only count toward the cap) is a reasonable but newly-made judgment call with no prior-phase precedent to check against; build-verification should confirm it doesn't produce a confusing UX where a user with a demo trip and one real trip can't tell why 'New Trip' is disabled or enabled.

The stress-trip perf/settlement test's pass/fail threshold for 'stays snappy' (named in tech_specs) still has not been quantified by this or any phase; M3's sign-off gate should either quantify it or treat it as correctness-only.

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: With Codex unavailable a ninth consecutive round, Claude's solo backend/systems pass turned the locked ten-milestone project plan into a concrete, buildable assignment package, adopted as the phase decision since it satisfies all three required acceptance checks (no ownerless task, acyclic dependencies, build workers can start immediately) without contradicting any prior-phase decision. The real Xcode project is placed at the app's own repo root (not orchestration scratch space) with four filesystem roots — WaypointKit/ (shared package), Waypoint/ (app UI), WaypointWidget/ (widget + Live Activity), WaypointTests/ — directly mirroring tech_specs' two-target-plus-package architecture. Ownership is enforced by subfolder path across the four fixed lanes: data_domain owns models/schema/persistence and initial scaffolding; services_utilities owns every plain service plus its own adversarial test suites as separate, independently-checkable tasks (so tests can't be silently skipped when a feature task is marked done); primary_ui owns the shared design-system components and all app-target screens; polish_resilience owns the entire widget/Live Activity target, StoreKit, privacy/accessibility, and the M9 degradation-verification checklist. project.pbxproj and WaypointKit/Package.swift are named the one unavoidable shared-edit forbidden zone, requiring sequential coordination and immediate integration rather than opportunistic concurrent edits. The output includes a 26-task acyclic backlog tracing every locked requirement (atomic reorder, integer-cents settlement, traveler-deletion guard, calendar dedup, iPad split view scoped to DayView, bounded Live Activity/widget verification, non-demo trip gating) to a specific file-owning task, and 8 flows-json user journeys giving the build-verification gate concrete, executable coverage of every primary promise rather than an improvised test plan.
open_risks: Codex has now missed nine consecutive phases due to rate-limiting/CLI unavailability; the entire path from product research through task assignment has had no genuine second-agent adversarial pass — this should be surfaced to a human reviewer before build execution begins in earnest, with M9 (build-verification) carrying the full weight of being the project's first real skeptical check.

The pbxproj/Package.swift sequential-coordination rule depends on lanes actually following it in practice during concurrent execution; if two lanes race to add files to the same target without checking in, this is the most likely source of a real merge conflict despite being called out explicitly.

Task T-017 (packing templates) and T-023 (StoreKit) are should-have/could-have scope respectively — if time-boxed, these are the correct tasks to drop per app_features' priority ordering, but the backlog itself doesn't visually flag that priority tier, so a build worker skimming tasks-json alone could misjudge which tasks are safe to defer under time pressure.

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: With Codex unavailable a tenth consecutive round, Claude's solo pass served as the final pre-build gate rather than another planning round, auditing prompt contract through tasks for real cross-phase contradictions rather than restating prior agreement. It found three concrete, fixable issues and no deeper architectural gaps: (1) task T-017 improperly bundled the must-have packing checklist with the should-have packing templates under joint acceptance criteria, undermining the point of app_features' must/should split — resolved by splitting into T-017a (checklist, must-have) and T-017b (templates, should-have, first cut under time pressure); (2) the term 'active trip' was locked with two incompatible meanings across the project (date-range-based for Live Activity/widget per ActiveTripResolver, vs. current-trip-count-based for the free-tier monetization gate per ios_architecture_review's actual implementation) — resolved by reserving 'active trip' for the date-range meaning only and renaming the monetization concept to 'trip slot'/'existing trip count' in all copy and docs; (3) T-025's build-verification task never explicitly named manual verification of the actual finger-drag gesture (as opposed to the automated Move-to-path regression test), despite ios_architecture_review having already decided that gesture requires manual verification — resolved by adding an explicit acceptance criterion requiring 5+ manually-exercised cross-day drags with no duplication/loss observed. All other locked guarantees (atomic move, integer-cents settlement, calendar dedup, App Group dual-purpose setup, iPad split scoped to DayView, non-demo trip gating) were confirmed consistent end to end with no drift. The phase's verdict is READY TO BUILD: none of the three fixes require reopening a locked decision, and the build phase can proceed without inventing new product/design/architecture decisions. The standing risk carried forward unresolved is that Codex has never reviewed any phase of this project, making M9 (build-verification) the project's first and only genuine adversarial check — this phase explicitly declined to let that risk block build start, but required it be stated plainly rather than softened.
open_risks: Codex has now missed ten consecutive phases due to rate-limiting/CLI unavailability; the entire product-through-build-readiness chain has had zero genuine second-agent adversarial review, placing full weight on M9 (build-verification) as the project's first real skeptical pass — this is a standing risk for the human reviewer to weigh, not something this phase could resolve.

The 'active trip' vs. 'trip slot' renaming is a naming-only fix at this phase; it must actually be applied consistently across all UI copy, code identifiers, and documentation during build, not just noted here and forgotten.

The T-017 split and T-025 acceptance-criteria addition are lightweight task-list edits that assume whoever executes M4 and M9 actually reads this phase's output rather than the original task_assignments transcript verbatim — a build worker working only from the old tasks-json block would miss both fixes.

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: Fourth diagnostic round on the 'DEMO caption never appears after toggle tap' UI-crawl gate failure produced a real, verified-by-direct-file-read code fix: SettingsView.swift's Demo Trip Toggle was restructured into its own Section (matching Apple's native Settings.app Section{Toggle} footer{Text} pattern instead of a shared hand-built VStack row), given an explicit .toggleStyle(.switch), and instrumented with OSLog diagnostics at the tap closure, DemoSeeder.seedIfNeeded's entry/success/failure paths, and DemoSeeder.remove's entry/success/failure paths, closing the prior round's blind spot where a clean success and a never-called function produced identical (silent) log output. The integrator (this phase) independently re-verified the landed diff against the real files in app_build rather than trusting the transcript: confirmed correct Trip/Day/Stop initializer usage, exactly one SettingsView definition, accessibilityIdentifiers bound directly to the interactive Toggle/Button controls (not wrapping containers), correct settings.tabButton/tripSwitcher.newTripButton wiring in TripSwitcherView.swift, zero application of the two fallback-model (Codex) responses' fabricated and broken code (invalid ModelContext(), bogus force-unwrapped UUID, double-toggling Button-wrapping-Toggle), and that DemoSeederTests.swift already unit-tests the seed/remove persistence logic successfully against a real in-memory ModelContext. The integrator also attempted to actually execute xcodebuild/swift build in this environment to get a live compile result beyond code review, but both remain blocked by the environment's tool-approval gate exactly as every prior round found — so despite this being the most thoroughly-verified fix yet (real file reads, not just transcript trust, plus passing unit tests on the data layer), no one has still ever watched the toggle visually flip or the DEMO caption appear on a live running build or crawl execution across this entire project's history.
open_risks: No live xcodebuild/simctl/crawl execution has ever occurred across this project's full history to confirm the Settings demo-toggle actually flips and the DEMO caption appears on a real running build — this remains the single highest-priority gap, now with full diagnostic logging in place to make the next live attempt conclusive.

If the next live run still shows the toggle failing to flip despite this round's structural fix and logging, the new OSLog lines should finally distinguish tap-never-reached vs render-observation-gap vs save-failure conclusively — but that distinguishing has still never actually been observed.

Overall app launch readiness remains a separate, still-open question from this narrow gate fix, per the standing project rule (DEC-final_review-002 and reaffirmed every review round since) against blending a narrow fix's own correctness with broader launch-readiness claims.

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: Round 2 fixed the compile failure build_verification caught after round 1 (TripLiveActivity.swift:93, 'some View' has no member 'ledgerValueStyle') by moving LedgerValueStyle/ledgerValueStyle() from the app-target-only Waypoint/Support/LedgerValueModifiers.swift into the shared WaypointKit/Sources/WaypointKit/LedgerValueModifiers.swift as public, following the same cross-target-sharing pattern already established for Theme/DemoStampBadge/CategoryPin (DEC-design_handoff-005) — the app-target file was left as an inert stub rather than deleted, to avoid a dangling pbxproj reference. Claude A and Claude B independently converged on the identical fix with no duplication. The round also closed a gap flagged across three prior rounds: TripGateChecker (WaypointKit/Sources/WaypointKit/Services/TripGateChecker.swift) now exists as a real pure function implementing the free-tier trip-count gate exactly per DEC-ios_architecture_review-013/DEC-project_plan-003/DEC-implementation_readiness_gate-002's 'trip slot' naming rule, with 5 passing-by-inspection unit tests in TripGateCheckerTests.swift — it is deliberately not yet wired into TripSwitcherView's New Trip button, which remains explicitly flagged as separate future work rather than silently assumed done. All three new/changed files this round sit in SwiftPM auto-globbed paths under WaypointKit, so no project.pbxproj or Package.swift changes were needed from the integrator. For the third consecutive round, a Codex fallback lane (Qwen2.5 Coder, since gpt-5.3-codex-spark was unavailable) reported writing a CalendarExportService.swift replacement with a fabricated EventKit API and an accompanying test file that wouldn't compile on its own terms — confirmed via git status to have never actually been written to disk, consistent with the two prior rounds' pattern; both Codex lanes also announced plans to build TripGateChecker despite it already existing, which would have caused a duplicate-declaration error had it actually landed. The integrator could not run an actual compile in this environment (xcodebuild/swift build require interactive approval unavailable in this non-interactive session) so the fix is verified by close manual code/import inspection, not a confirmed green build.
open_risks: The LedgerValueStyle fix has not been confirmed by an actual compile in this environment — it is verified by manual code inspection (import statements, call sites, public access modifiers all check out) but build_verification's next real xcodebuild run against the actual toolchain is still the first authoritative confirmation.

TripGateChecker is fully implemented and tested but not called from anywhere in the UI yet — TripSwitcherView's 'New Trip' button remains completely ungated, so the free-tier trip-count limit described throughout product/architecture phases has no enforcement in the running app despite the underlying logic now existing and being correct.

The Codex/Qwen2.5 fallback lane has now produced the same fabricated CalendarExportService.swift rewrite (with a non-existent EventKit authorization-status-enum API) across three consecutive rounds, plus a proposal to duplicate-build TripGateChecker after it already existed — its reports should continue to be treated as unverified narrative requiring a filesystem check before any action is taken on them.

No round of this build's entire history has had a confirmed successful xcodebuild/swift build run in this actual sandboxed environment — every fix, this round included, is verified by manual review only, so an unexpected second-order compile error (e.g. an access-level or import issue not caught by inspection) remains possible until a real build actually runs.

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: build_verification closed with the project's first tool-confirmed build result: VERIFIED (xcodebuild) — compiled cleanly for the iOS Simulator, after twelve-plus phases where every prior claim was manual code review only. Codex (running as Qwen2.5 fallback) proposed in round 1 wiring TripGateChecker into the New Trip button and re-running a full test-for-testing pass as 'next steps'; Claude pushed back and, after Codex went into rate-limit cooldown for round 2 and did not rebut, the objection stood: this phase's rules permit only repairing compile/test failures with minimal changes and explicitly forbid new feature work, and TripGateChecker/LiveActivityController being unwired was already named as deferred future work in a prior phase (write_tests round 2), not a defect discovered here, so wiring either now would be scope creep — especially undesirable given the Qwen2.5 fallback lane's history of fabricating a nonexistent EventKit API across three prior rounds elsewhere in this project. Claude independently attempted, across both rounds, to get a tool-confirmed signal on test execution (swift test --package-path WaypointKit, then xcodebuild ... build-for-testing) and on running the project's 8 flows-json user journeys (cross-day drag, 5-traveler settle-up, forced MKDirections failure, calendar export/re-export, demo toggle) against a live Simulator; both attempts were blocked by the same sandbox interactive-approval wall that has blocked every prior round's self-verification in this project. The phase's final position, adopted without contradiction: report build status (PASS, confirmed) and test-execution status (UNVERIFIED, blocked) as two separate facts rather than one blended VERIFIED, perform no new feature work, and carry forward five concrete, named honest blockers for final review: Live Activity has zero call sites and never fires; the free-tier trip-count gate (TripGateChecker) is implemented and tested but unenforced in the running app; calendar export has no automated test coverage despite its must-have justification; automated XCTest suite pass/fail status is unconfirmed; and none of the 8 locked flows-json user journeys have ever been executed against a running build.
open_risks: Test-execution status (whether WaypointKitTests/WaypointTests — including the settlement adversarial suite and the 10x/20x cross-day reorder regression test — actually ran and passed) remains unconfirmed; this sandbox environment appears structurally unable to provide that signal, so final review must either find a way to get tool access or explicitly accept build-only verification as the ceiling here.

None of the 8 flows-json user journeys locked in task_assignments have ever been executed against a running Simulator across the entire project history; this was attempted and blocked this round, not skipped, but it means no primary user-facing promise (drag integrity, settlement math, calendar dedup, honest map degradation, demo toggle) has been observed working end-to-end in a live build.

Live Activity, the free-tier trip-count gate, and calendar export test coverage are all real, unassigned gaps beneath the clean compile — no future phase has yet explicitly been given ownership of closing them, so they risk falling through the cracks unless final review assigns them.

The Qwen2.5/Codex fallback lane's reliability remains a standing concern for any future phase that assigns it file-editing work, given its repeated fabrication pattern (a nonexistent EventKit API proposed three consecutive rounds in write_tests) and this round's proposal to take on UI wiring work that was out of this phase's scope.

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: This phase produced Waypoint's manual simulator/device QA script, adopted from Claude's round-1 draft (rigorous and grounded in build_verification's actual findings) over Codex's round-1 draft (generic/templated, and containing a factual error — a full subscription/paywall testing section against StoreKit UI that build_coordination confirmed was never built). The final checklist opens with a mandatory pre-flight crash gate for the App Group entitlement error build_verification's test run actually hit, since that same App Group backs SwiftData persistence and the widget/debug-date hook — if it reproduces, the report must say most of the checklist is blocked rather than quietly testing only what still runs. Coverage spans: onboarding and the demo-trip singleton toggle (including rapid on/off cycling and the visible DEMO stamp requirement); trip date-range math including single-day trips, extend-vs-shrink-guard behavior, and the 7-day ribbon compact-mode switch that's never been visually confirmed; cross-day drag-reorder tested via both the finger-drag gesture and the accessible 'Move to...' path with VoiceOver, each checked against the identical atomic end state across 10+ rapid moves; map routing's honest approximate-route fallback and two-way pin/list selection; expense logging across all three split methods with 5+ travelers, inline rejection of non-100%-summing percentages, and manual verification of the settle-up screen's three distinct states and cent-exact arithmetic; packing checklist correctness; calendar export's created/updated counts, re-export dedup verified directly in the Calendar app, externally-deleted-event handling, and permission-denied handling; iPad two-pane split view across 2+ sizes, both orientations, and a mid-session rotation, scoped correctly to the day view only; accessibility (VoiceOver full-app navigation, largest Dynamic Type with a hard no-clipping rule for times/money, light/dark contrast); persistence including force-quit mid-drag and mid-expense-entry, not just clean close/reopen; offline/Airplane-Mode functional testing; and release-build hygiene confirming the debug date-override hook is excluded from Release builds. Two features confirmed unbuilt/unwired by build_verification — Live Activity (zero call sites) and the free-tier trip-count gate (TripGateChecker implemented but never called from the New Trip button) — get honest 'confirm no crash, no fake success' steps and are logged explicitly as open regressions in a Known Gaps section, rather than being tested as if working or silently omitted. StoreKit/paywall testing was removed from the checklist body entirely and replaced with an explicit not-applicable note, correcting Codex's draft.
open_risks: The App Group entitlement crash from build_verification has not actually been re-tested or fixed by this phase — this checklist's step 0 is the first place anyone will find out whether it still reproduces, and if it does, the bulk of this checklist becomes unexecutable until a future phase fixes the entitlement.

This checklist has never actually been executed end-to-end by a human or automated harness in this sandboxed environment — like every prior phase, its steps are authored and reasoned about but not run, so its own correctness (e.g., whether the described UI elements exist with the exact behavior assumed) is unconfirmed.
Live Activity and the trip-count gate remain real, unassigned functional gaps with no future phase yet named as owning the fix — this QA script documents them but doesn't resolve them.

Codex's fabricated paywall-testing content was caught and corrected within this same round, but it's the same fallback-lane pattern (fabricating features/APIs that don't exist) that has recurred across at least four prior phases in this project — any future phase reusing Codex/Qwen output should keep verifying claims against the actual filesystem/build state rather than trusting the narrative.

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: This phase produced Waypoint's App Store launch-readiness package, adopted from Claude's round-1 draft after it directly corrected several factual errors in Codex's (Qwen2.5 fallback) draft: Codex proposed declaring Location Services, Contacts, and HealthKit privacy usage strings despite the locked architecture never requesting location permission and the app never using Contacts/HealthKit at all; Codex wrote a subscription/paywall review-risk section as if a paywall exists despite StoreKit being confirmed entirely unbuilt; and Codex fabricated a support email and phone number that don't exist anywhere in this project. The adopted final output declares the app NOT YET launch-ready but close, with five sequenced blockers: confirm the App Group entitlement crash (surfaced in build_verification) doesn't reproduce on a real cold app launch, not just the test target; get at least one live execution of the core human_qa_checklist flows (crash gate, drag-reorder, settlement, calendar export) since no primary claim in this app has ever been observed working outside code review; explicitly decide Live Activity's fate (wire its two remaining call sites or keep it fully out of marketing copy, screenshots, and keywords — the default chosen here); produce a real support URL and privacy policy URL, currently missing entirely; and run a genuine iPad visual pass before any iPad screenshot is used. Privacy labels are locked as 'Data Not Collected' everywhere except Calendar (full access, not linked to identity/tracking), with no Location/Contacts/HealthKit entries. The app ships as fully free with zero IAP/paywall copy, since TripGateChecker exists but is never called, meaning every real user currently gets unlimited trips regardless of any future tier plan. A five-screenshot plan was locked (day view with DEMO stamp, settle-up ledger arithmetic, map approximate-route fallback, packing checklist, calendar export confirmation), explicitly excluding an iPad screenshot until verified.
open_risks: The App Group entitlement crash has not actually been re-tested against a real (non-test-target) app launch by this phase — it's named as the top blocker but remains unconfirmed either way.

None of the 8 flows-json user journeys or the human_qa_checklist's core sections have ever been executed against a live build across this entire project's history; every launch-readiness claim in this phase's output rests on code review, not observation.

Live Activity's fate (wire vs. permanently exclude from marketing) is still an open product decision for whoever owns the next build round — this phase only decided how to handle it in copy for the current unwired state.

The support URL / privacy policy URL is named as a required pre-submission task but has not been created by any phase to date — submission is blocked on this pure-paperwork item until someone actually produces it.

Codex's fallback lane (Qwen2.5) has again produced content contradicted by the project's own locked architecture decisions (location permission, unused-capability privacy declarations) and fabricated contact information — consistent with its pattern across many prior phases, reinforcing that its claims need independent verification before use.

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: This review round confirmed, with a single-reviewer perspective (Codex declined to answer rather than fabricate, a genuine improvement over its prior UIKit-flavored fabrications but still leaving no independent second opinion), that the demo-toggle Section restructure and control-exposure fixes landed in build_coordination and iterate_scope are well-formed and independently verified by direct file reads across two phases, with a clean xcodebuild compile. This narrow fix is accepted as GO on its own terms. The overall app launch verdict remains NO-GO, unchanged since DEC-final_review-001: seven of eight core prompt features are solidly built and code-reviewed (trips/itinerary date math, map with MKDirections/fallback, debt-simplification settlement math, packing, calendar export dedup, iPad split view, widget), Live Activity is reported to now have real call sites (an upgrade from fully-coded-but-dormant, though still unobserved running), and StoreKit remains intentionally unbuilt. The standing blockers are unchanged and reaffirmed: the App Group cold-launch entitlement question has never been tested via a real (non-test) app-scheme cold launch with console observation; zero live execution of any of the 8 flows.json journeys or the human_qa_checklist has ever occurred against a running build across this project's entire history; the flows.json widget/Live Activity assertion rewrite (decided in iterate_scope) has never been confirmed applied at the orchestration layer outside this repo; and the in-app Gaps section's reachability by an actual user remains unconfirmed. The review's central message, reaffirmed from the prior round: further code-level diagnosis has diminishing value at this point — the single highest-priority next action is simply running the app once, live, and observing what happens.
open_risks: The App Group cold-launch entitlement question remains completely untested against the real app scheme and could still block everything downstream, including the demo-toggle fix, the moment anyone actually runs it.

No live crawl or QA-checklist execution has ever happened in this project's history; all functional-correctness claims (settlement math, drag integrity, calendar dedup, demo toggle, iPad split view) rest on code review and static reasoning only.

The flows.json orchestration-layer file needed to make the release gate pass end-to-end has never been confirmed updated with the already-decided widget/Live Activity assertion rewrite, meaning even a fully correct app-side fix may not be sufficient for the gate to go green.
The in-app Gaps section required by the original prompt has never been confirmed reachable by an actual user, despite being discussed at the orchestration layer for many phases running.

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: Portfolio audit was marked not applicable for Waypoint: the original prompt names one product, and portfolio_selection locked a single-app decision early in the project's lifecycle with a rationale that has never been reopened — the settlement/reorder/calendar-dedup guarantees all depend on one shared SwiftData model, so splitting into sibling apps would duplicate state across process boundaries for no benefit. There is no portfolio-json manifest, no sibling app folders, and no child prompts to check for preserved requirements, because none of that structure was ever created or warranted. The WidgetKit extension (which also hosts Live Activity via ActivityConfiguration) is explicitly a target within the single Waypoint Xcode project, not a sibling portfolio app, consistent with ios_architecture_review's 'two targets total' correction. Both Claude (round 1) and the coordinator independently attempted a direct filesystem check for stray duplicate Waypoint-named directories outside the known four project roots (Waypoint.xcodeproj, WaypointKit/, Waypoint/, WaypointWidget/, WaypointTests/) and were both blocked by sandbox scope restrictions limiting access to .agent_cwd only; this is recorded as attempted-and-blocked rather than silently passed or silently skipped, in keeping with this project's established discipline of not claiming verification that was only reasoned about. Given ten-plus phases of completely consistent references to exactly those four filesystem roots with no contradicting mention anywhere in the project's history, this is assessed as low residual risk, not a live open question. No backfill-to-Jira/Notion action applies since there is no child-project structure; any follow-up items from prior phases' blocker lists should be filed within Waypoint's own single project tracker.
open_risks: A direct filesystem check confirming no stray duplicate Waypoint-named directory exists outside the known project roots has never actually been run in this project's history — both attempts this phase were blocked by sandbox scope, so this remains inferred-but-unconfirmed rather than observed, consistent with this project's broader pattern of design-intent-confirmed-but-not-observed claims.

This phase, like most in this project's history, proceeded with Codex unavailable for its entire duration, meaning the portfolio-applicability call itself has had no independent second-agent review — though the underlying single-app decision it's confirming (portfolio_selection) did have genuine two-agent consensus much earlier in the project.

summaries.one_paragraph_summary: This round investigated a second UI-crawl gate failure: after the earlier control-exposure fix (settings.tabButton/Done/tripSwitcher.newTripButton) landed and passed, the 'Honest first launch, then enable demo trip' flow now fails one step later — after tapping settings.demoTripToggle, the expected 'DEMO' caption text never appears, and the captured screenshot still shows the pre-toggle OFF state. Rather than guessing a fix, the group established that this requires a three-way diagnostic, not the human's original two-way framing: (1) the tap never actually landed on the real Toggle control (a tap-targeting/identifier-binding problem, identical in a screenshot to a state-propagation failure), (2) the switch's own visual state flipped but the caption is reading a stale/different source of truth (a SwiftUI render-observation gap), or (3) the switch flipped optimistically but the underlying demo trip was never actually persisted (a genuine save-race bug in setDemoTrip(enabled:)/DemoSeeder, which would be a live violation of the project's own 'never claim an outcome that hasn't happened' rule). Codex's fallback-model response proposed a UIKit-flavored (@IBAction/UISwitch/DispatchQueue.asyncAfter) patch that does not correspond to this SwiftUI/SwiftData project's actual architecture and was rejected as fabricated, repeating a failure pattern already flagged in final_review. This session independently re-confirmed it has no filesystem access to the real Waypoint project (direct find/ls attempts blocked to an empty .agent_cwd), so no hypothesis could be empirically settled here; instead, the phase locked the diagnostic procedure and the scoped, per-hypothesis fix for whichever cause is actually confirmed, deferring execution to whoever next has real build access.
open_risks: The actual root cause (tap-targeting vs. render-observation gap vs. genuine save-race bug in setDemoTrip/DemoSeeder) remains undiagnosed pending real build/filesystem access — this phase could only specify the diagnostic and per-outcome fix, not perform it.

If the root cause turns out to be hypothesis 3 (genuine save-race bug), this is a live instance of the app's own 'never claim an outcome that hasn't happened' violation in its most trust-sensitive first-run feature, and should be treated with corresponding priority once diagnosed.

This gate failure is downstream of the still-unresolved App Group cold-launch entitlement risk (DEC-final_review-001/DEC-final_review3-004); if that crash reproduces on real-app-scheme launch, it would block diagnosing this issue at all, not just narrow its scope.
